title: INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE
body:
The first programming course in the degree, taught in [[Python]]. It is about the part of
programming that is not a language: how you turn a problem you have been handed into a sequence
of steps a machine can execute, and how you find out when you have got it wrong. The language is
the excuse; [[Algorithm|algorithmic thinking]], [[Pseudocode|planning before coding]], and
[[Tracing Table|tracing what the code actually does]] are the content, and all three outlast
Python.

> [!note] The course number changed and this file did not
> This is now **COMP 1701, Introduction to Problem Solving and Programming**, the unified first
> course for both Computer Science and Computer Information Systems majors at Mount Royal. It
> **replaced COMP 1631 and COMP 1501**, which were separate entry-level courses. The folder and
> filename keep the old number because that is what Evan took, and every existing link points
> here. `COMP 1701` is an alias on this note, so searching that number lands you in the right
> place.

**Most of what this course teaches already has a note in
[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]]**, written in C a year later: variables, functions, scope,
decisions, loops, errors, lists, files. That is an accident of when the vault started, not a
judgement about where the material belongs. **This parent links across rather than duplicating**,
the same handoff [[C]] makes to that course from [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]]. What lives in this
folder is the twelve notes that are genuinely Python's or genuinely nobody's.

## Topics

### Problem solving and algorithmic thinking

[[Algorithm]] · [[Pseudocode]] · [[Tracing Table]] · [[Program design]] · [[IPO Diagram]] ·
[[Structure chart]] · [[Function design]]

The actual subject of the course. [[Algorithm]] carries Polya's four steps (understand, plan,
implement, test) and the properties an algorithm has to have: ordered, explicit, effective,
complete. [[Pseudocode]] is step two made concrete, precise about logic and silent about syntax,
and it exists so that a logic mistake costs one line instead of a debugging session.

[[Tracing Table]] is the one to actually practise. You execute the code by hand, one row per
step, one column per variable, with the loop condition in its own column, and it is the only
technique that finds a [[Logic Errors|logic error]] when there is no error message to read.

[[IPO Diagram]] asks what goes in and what comes out, [[Structure chart]] asks how the functions
divide the work, [[Program design]] is the whole procedure. Each answers a different question and
none of them replaces writing the thing down.

### The machine underneath

[[Hardware]] · [[Processor]] · [[Machine Language]] · [[Interpriting]] · [[Compiling]] ·
[[Memory]]

High-level exposure only, and the one distinction that pays off immediately is
[[Interpriting]] against [[Compiling]]: both end in [[Machine Language]], but Python translates
and runs at the same time, so there is no build step and no executable. That is why the edit-run
cycle is fast, why the source has to be present every time, and why it is slower.
[[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] is where all of this is taken seriously.

### Python, and what dynamic typing costs

[[Python]] · [[Data type]] · [[Variable]] · [[Type casting]] · [[Integer]] · [[Float]] ·
[[String]] · [[Boolean]] · [[Augmented Assignment]] · [[Style Conventions]] · [[Input]] ·
[[Output]]

[[Python]] is the contrast note and the three decisions in it explain everything else: it is
interpreted, it is dynamically typed, and its indentation is syntax rather than style.

**Dynamic typing is the big one.** A [[Variable]] here is a name bound to a value, and the value
carries the type, so a name can be rebound to something else entirely and nothing complains until
an operation fails. What C catches at compile time, Python discovers at run time or never. That
is the argument for [[Test Coverage]] rather than against it.

[[Input]] and [[Output]] have notes in COMP 1633; the Python-specific trap is that `input()`
always returns a [[String]], so [[Type casting]] to `int` or `float` comes first and forgetting is
the first real bug most people write. [[Augmented Assignment]] (`+=`) is shorthand worth learning
early because it stops `x = x + 1` looking like an equation. [[Style Conventions]] are graded in
this course because in Python the layout *is* the code.

### Decisions

[[Descision]] · [[Conditional]] · [[Comparison Operators]] · [[Logical Operators]] ·
[[Boolean]] · [[Dangling else]] · [[Switch]]

`if` / `elif` / `else`, which COMP 1633 owns as [[Descision]] and [[Conditional]]. The two notes
here are the operators that build the condition: [[Comparison Operators]] for the six that
produce a [[Boolean]] (and the `=` against `==` mistake), [[Logical Operators]] for `not`, `and`,
`or`, their precedence, and **short-circuit evaluation**, which is the one that is a technique
rather than a detail: `if count != 0 and total / count > 10` is safe only because the second half
never runs when the first is False.

Those three operators are AND, OR, and NOT from [[Boolean Algebra]], and De Morgan's laws work
here exactly as they do in a circuit.

### Repetition

[[Repetition]] · [[While loop]] · [[For loop]] · [[Control variable]] · [[Loop design]] ·
[[Infinite loop]] · [[Finite loop]] · [[Counted loop]] · [[Nested loop]] · [[Accumulator]] ·
[[Sentinel]]

**Entirely owned by [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] and nothing new was written here.**
The material transfers unchanged: a [[While loop]] tests, executes, and repeats;
[[Control variable]] has to be initialised, evaluated, and updated, and missing any of the three
gives an [[Infinite loop]]; [[Accumulator]] is the running-total pattern that
[[Augmented Assignment]] is the notation for.

The course's own emphasis is iteration bounds, which is a [[Tracing Table]] exercise: how many
times does this actually run, and is the answer off by one.

### Functions and modules

[[Function]] · [[Function design]] · [[Parameter]] · [[Formal parameter]] ·
[[Actual parameter]] · [[Variable Scope]] · [[Docstring]] · [[Standard Library]] · [[Library]] ·
[[Void]]

Value-returning against non-value-returning is the split, and [[Void]] in COMP 1633 is the note
for the second kind: a function that does its work through side effects rather than a return
value. [[Variable Scope]] is local against global, and it is the same idea in both languages even
though the rules differ.

[[Docstring]] is the Python-specific one and it is **not a comment**: it survives into the running
program, so `help(f)` prints it. [[Standard Library]] covers `math`, `random`, and `turtle`, and
carries the point that `random` is a seeded pseudo-random generator, not randomness, which is
[[Random Numbers]] in [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]].

### Errors, testing, debugging

[[Errors]] · [[Compile Errors]] · [[Runtime Errors]] · [[Logic Errors]] · [[debugging]] ·
[[Driver]] · [[Test Coverage]] · [[Unit testing]]

[[Errors]] owns the taxonomy and it transfers with one real change: **Python has no compile
step**, so syntax errors are raised by the parser and the type mismatches C catches at compile
time become [[Runtime Errors]] here. [[Logic Errors]] are identical, because no language catches
those.

[[Test Coverage]] is the new note and it answers the question [[Unit testing]] and [[Driver]] do
not: which inputs. Partition into classes, test one from each, **then test every boundary and the
value either side of it**, because `>` against `>=` is invisible at 75 and obvious at 50.

### Lists and files

[[Python List]] · [[List]] · [[Array]] · [[Index]] · [[File I-O]] · [[File]] · [[String]]

[[List]] in COMP 1633 is the [[Abstract Data Type]] and already hands off to this course by name;
[[Python List]] is the concrete built-in with the [[Implementation]] hidden. The comparison that
matters: a Python list grows, holds mixed types, indexes from the right, slices, and **raises
`IndexError` instead of reading whatever is next in memory**. The C version is faster and this is
the one to learn on.

[[File I-O]] is open, process, close, with `with` doing the closing. Two things always catch
people: everything read from a file is a [[String]], and lines keep their trailing newline.

## Core Facts to Know

- Polya's four steps: understand the problem, plan, implement, then test and improve.
- Pseudocode commits to the logic and refuses to commit to syntax; that is the point, not a
  limitation.
- A [[Tracing Table]] gives the loop condition its own column, because off-by-one bugs live in
  the gap between the test and the update.
- Python is **interpreted**: no build step, no executable, source needed at every run.
- Python is **dynamically typed**: values carry types, names do not.
- It is also **strongly** typed: `5 + "five"` raises `TypeError`, it does not coerce.
- Indentation delimits blocks, so whitespace is syntax and misalignment is a bug.
- `input()` always returns a [[String]]. Convert before doing arithmetic.
- `=` assigns, `==` compares.
- Logical operator precedence: `not`, then `and`, then `or`.
- `and` / `or` **short-circuit**: the right operand is not evaluated when the left decides the
  answer. This is what makes a guard clause work.
- A [[Control variable]] needs initialising, evaluating, and updating; miss one and the loop never
  ends.
- A [[Docstring]] is not a comment: it stays in the program and `help()` prints it.
- `random` is pseudo-random and seeded, so a program using it is still reproducible.
- Three error classes: syntax (parse time), runtime (execution), logic (never reported).
- Python has no compile step, so type errors are runtime errors, and an unexecuted branch never
  reports one.
- Test boundaries and the values either side of them; that is where `>` against `>=` shows.
- Testing shows the presence of bugs, never their absence.
- A Python list is mutable, heterogeneous, growable, and bounds-checked.
- `b = a` aliases a list, `b = a[:]` copies it. This is [[Call by reference]] arriving a year
  early.
- Opening a file with mode `"w"` truncates it immediately, with no warning.
- Everything read from a file is a string, and it keeps its newline.

## Related courses

- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] (COMP 1633) is the sequel and **owns most of this
  material in C**: [[Variable]], [[Function]], [[Variable Scope]], [[Data type]], [[Descision]],
  [[Repetition]], [[Errors]], [[List]], [[Array]], [[File]]. The relationship is the point of
  both courses: the same ideas with the machine visible. [[Pointer]], [[Memory]],
  [[Stack and Heap]], and [[Dynamic Allocation]] are what Python was hiding.
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] (COMP 2631) asks what a list *costs*, which this course deliberately
  does not: [[Time Complexity]], [[Linked List]], [[Hashing]].
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] (COMP 2655) takes [[Hardware]], [[Processor]], and
  [[Machine Language]] seriously, and [[C]] there is written as the translation table between a
  language and the machine.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]] (COMP 2633) is where [[Unit testing]],
  [[Coupling and Cohesion]], and the testing-versus-proof argument get their real treatment.
- [[PROGRAMMING PARADIGMS]]: Python is procedural here and multi-paradigm in general, and the
  fact that functions are objects is where that course starts.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] (MATH 2303) and [[MACHINE LEARNING]] are where Python comes
  back as the working language of the degree rather than a teaching one.
- [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]]: [[Random Numbers]] for what `random` actually is, and
  [[Algorithm]]'s properties are its opening chapter.
